claims.text: Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al can be produced by directed energy deposition, and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 can be produced as a coating by laser cladding.
The proposed initial refractory high-entropy alloy is predominantly a single-phase solid solution.
The proposed initial alloy has a relatively fine grain size.
Y and Hf can be co-doped into an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 high-entropy-alloy coating during laser cladding.
Y and Hf co-doping is applicable to refractory high-entropy alloys generally, including Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al.
A 900 °C exposure in 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl molten salt is an experimentally established condition for Y-Hf-co-doped AlCoCrFeNi2.1 coatings.
Y and Hf co-doping will refine the grain structure relative to an undoped alloy.
Y and Hf co-doping reduces grain coarsening during a 900 °C, 10-hour heat treatment.
Y and Hf preferentially segregate to grain boundaries.
Segregated Y and Hf act as grain-boundary pinning agents that limit high-temperature grain coarsening.
Y and Hf stabilize secondary-phase precipitates in the alloy.
Stable secondary-phase precipitates inhibit grain growth.
Precipitate strengthening and a refined grain structure enhance load transfer and creep resistance.
Y-Hf co-doping improves the thermal stability of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 coatings at 900 °C.
The co-doped alloy will have greater microhardness at 900 °C than an otherwise identical undoped alloy.
The co-doped alloy will have greater yield strength at 900 °C than an otherwise identical undoped alloy.
The mechanical-property improvement will hold in corrosive molten-salt environments similar to 75% Na2SO4 and 25% NaCl.
The proposed effect is expected to hold for refractory high-entropy alloys at temperatures up to approximately 900 °C.
Unwanted phase formation may offset the benefits of Y and Hf co-doping.

contradictions.description: The conditions field calls for room-temperature baseline measurements, whereas the stated baseline and predicted outcome require comparison between doped and undoped alloys at 900 °C. These are different comparison baselines.
